prompt.context: Arendelia Pharmaceuticals is a fast growing, innovative pharmaceutical company that has developed best-in-class treatments for Frozen Heart Syndrome (FHS), a rare but devastating progressive disease that significantly shortens a patient's lifespan without treatment. Arendelia had $6.2B in revenue in 2020 and grew revenues 55% from 2019 to 2020. Arendelia has hired your firm to understand whether or not its current growth is sustainable and what they should do to ensure long term growth.
prompt.question: Is Arendelia's current growth sustainable, and what should they do to ensure long-term growth?

clarifying_info.q: What type of company is Arendelia?
clarifying_info.a: A US biopharmaceutical company founded in 1989 which focuses on delivering scientifically innovative treatments for diseases with high unmet need.

clarifying_info.q: How large is the FHS patient population?
clarifying_info.a: There are an estimated 100k total patients with FHS worldwide: 70% in the US, 30% international. YoY growth rates are correlated with population growth at approximately 1% annually.

clarifying_info.q: Does Arendelia have competition in the FHS market?
clarifying_info.a: Arendelia has a monopoly on the FHS market as they are the only product that treats the underlying cause of FHS rather than the symptoms. Competition is likely in the future but not a current concern.

clarifying_info.q: What products does Arendelia sell and at what price?
clarifying_info.a: Arendelia sells 4 products to treat FHS, each priced at $300k/year in the US and $100k/year internationally.
Products are room temperature stable pills making them easy to ship and store. Patients take 1 pill 2x daily for their entire lives.

clarifying_info.q: When are FHS patients typically diagnosed?
clarifying_info.a: FHS is typically diagnosed at a very young age and most eligible patients with healthcare coverage are treated with one of Arendelia's products.

exhibits.title: Product Revenues (M) vs % of FHS Patients Eligible for Arendelia's Products
exhibits.shows: A dual-axis chart showing Arendelia's annual product revenues (stacked bars by product: FHS-1, FHS-2, FHS-3, FHS-4) from 2012 to 2020 alongside the percentage of FHS patients eligible for one or more of Arendelia's products (line). Products were launched in 2012, 2015, 2017, and 2019 respectively.

exhibits.title: Pipeline Products for Potential Investment
exhibits.shows: A table of six pipeline products (A through F) across different disease areas showing clinical trial phase, synergy with current strategy, projected lifetime product revenue ($B), cost of development ($B), likelihood of approval, and acquisition price ($B) where applicable. The company has a $15B budget to invest across R&D and M&A.

framework: Organic Growth - Current Products: assess price increases vs. volume growth (new markets, new customers)
Organic Growth - New Products: develop pipeline assets within or adjacent to FHS
Inorganic Growth: M&A or licensing to enter new disease areas and diversify revenue

questions.prompt: Given that most eligible patients get on treatment within 2 years, are current revenue growth rates sustainable? (Exhibit 1)
questions.guidance: Strong answer: At 90% eligibility the patient pool is nearly saturated. With only ~1% annual population growth and no meaningful untreated population remaining, FHS revenues will plateau. Price increases are ruled out by public/regulatory pressure. Therefore 55% YoY growth is not sustainable from FHS alone, and Arendelia must diversify into new disease areas. Candidate may note each new product launch corresponded with a jump in both eligible % and revenues -- but that lever is now largely exhausted.

math.setup: Optional check: 100k patients worldwide, 70% US = 70k US patients. At $300k/year each, max US revenue = 70k x 300k = $21B. At 90% eligible and treated, ~$18.9B US ceiling. Combined with international this illustrates a ceiling exists, though exact calculation is not required.
steps: 70,000 US patients x $300,000 = $21B theoretical US max revenue
30,000 international patients x $100,000 = $3B theoretical international max revenue
At 90% eligibility: ~$21.6B total ceiling vs. $6.2B current -- still headroom but limited given 1% population growth
55% YoY growth would require ~$9.6B in 2021, meaning far more patients than currently treated in one year -- not achievable
math.answer: Current 55% growth rates are not sustainable; revenues will plateau as the eligible patient pool is ~90% penetrated and population growth is only ~1% annually.

questions.prompt: The co-founders have allocated $15B to invest in R&D and M&A. Which of the six pipeline products (A-F) should Arendelia pursue? (Exhibit 2)
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute expected value (EV) for each product and compare against total cost (R&D + acquisition price). EV formula: EV = (Projected revenues - Dev costs) * likelihood of success + (0 - Dev costs) * (1 - likelihood of success). Acquisition price is included in budget planning but is a sunk cost once made and excluded from EV. Correct answer: Select D, C, and A -- total cost $13B (within $15B budget), combined EV $21.5B. Second-order insight: phase correlates with likelihood (Phase 1 = 25%, Phase 2 = 50%, Phase 3 = 75%). Products B and D have identical revenue and dev cost projections but D is Phase 3 vs B at Phase 1 -- D is far superior. Product E has highest potential revenue but costs $14B alone (exceeds remaining budget after any other choice) and only 25% success probability.

math.setup: EV = (Revenue - Dev Cost) * P(success) + (0 - Dev Cost) * (1 - P(success)). Total Budget Cost for each = Dev Cost + Acquisition Price (if any).
steps: Select D ($6B) + C ($2B) + A ($5B) = $13B total -- within $15B budget
math.answer: Select Products A, C, and D. Total investment = $13B (under $15B budget). Combined expected value = $21.5B with max upside of $50B if all three are approved.

brainstorming.prompt: What should Arendelia consider before confirming their decision to branch out to other disease areas?

categories.name: Risks
ideas: Unfamiliarity with the science and market in a new disease area
FHS patients may be concerned about losing Arendelia's single-disease focus
Expanding too quickly could stretch internal resources -- financial and personnel -- too thin
Chosen products may not receive FDA approval

categories.name: Opportunities
ideas: Allows for larger and faster growth beyond the FHS patient ceiling
Diversifies the revenue portfolio reducing dependence on a single disease
Protects the firm from eventual competition in the FHS market and loss of exclusivity (LOE) on FHS patents

categories.name: Additional Revenue Diversification Options
ideas: License IP or technology to other pharma companies
Form joint ventures in new therapeutic areas
Sell non-core IP assets to fund higher-priority pipeline

categories.name: Go-to-Market Considerations
ideas: US vs. international launch sequencing given pricing and reimbursement differences
Reimbursement and payer negotiations for new disease areas
Supply chain readiness for new product forms or delivery mechanisms

recommendation: Invest in disease areas beyond Frozen Heart Syndrome to maximize future growth, as FHS revenues will plateau with ~90% patient eligibility already achieved
Use the $15B allocated budget to invest in Products A, C, and D for an expected value of $21.5B and maximum potential revenue of $50B
risks: Products A, C, or D may not receive FDA approval, eliminating or reducing the expected revenue upside
The acquisition of Product D may encounter deal execution difficulties or regulatory scrutiny
Entering unfamiliar disease areas introduces scientific and commercial execution risk
next_steps: Conduct robust due diligence on the Product D acquisition target before committing
Continuously monitor clinical trial data for Products A, C, and D to make informed go/no-go decisions at each phase transition
Develop a go-to-market strategy for new disease areas including reimbursement, pricing, and commercial infrastructure planning
